answer.evidence: The silhouette widens gradually from 10 px at row 1 to 63 px by row 27, so the roof reads as a long sloped plane seen from above. Horizontal rib lines at rows 7, 13, 20, 26 and 33 run across it. A dark eave line sits at rows 81-82 above the door. Below it is a vertical front face (rows 83-110) with an arched frame, glass double door and planters. The darker purple band on the right is curved-roof shading, not a separate side face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a vinyl greenhouse: a pale translucent barrel vault with a few green plant dots and a lower frame and door. Its main material ramp (the vinyl) has about 4 steps, with soft vertical banding and a highlight stripe, against 5-6 in the references' roof tiles, plaster and stone. Visible tones per tile are 8 vs 12 and 10 in the references, so it is lower but not drastically. Near-flat coverage is 25% vs 0% in both references, and the plain pale vinyl panels and the lower wall have flat areas with little grain. Only 16% of dark edge pixels are neutral (refs 7% and 9%), so the outline leans tinted/grey-blue rather than pure black. The frame and arch edges look selective, but the lower frame outline looks a bit uniform. Overall it is cleanly drawn and acceptable as a simpler object, but it is thinner and flatter than the references, with less per-tile grain. Since the instruction says to fail when in doubt, it falls short.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a vinyl greenhouse with a pale translucent barrel-vault shell. Its measured visible tones per tile are 8, against 12 and 10 for the references, so it is lower but not far below. Its near-flat coverage is 25%, while both references sit at 0%. The shell has a few banded highlight steps (about 4 lightness steps) and small leaf clusters on the plants inside, but the large smooth areas of the vault and the lower wall are close to flat. The sparse, translucent subject justifies some simplicity, but the flat panels and the shallower ramps would look thinner next to the references, so it fails under the when-in-doubt rule.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a vinyl greenhouse, a different structure from the tiled-roof houses, but it is still a whole building, so the kind matches. Its shading is fairly shallow: the translucent dome has about 4 pale steps (highlight, light, mid, shadow) plus a few green plant dots, against 5-6 steps per material on the references. Outline: the dark edge pixels are only 16% neutral, so the edges lean tinted, but the frame is a thin grey-green line with little material-toned darkening, which I call mixed. Texture: there are some ribbing lines, plant clusters and base dirt, but nothing like the per-tile scallops and plaster speckle on the references. Measured: 8 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 for the references, and 25% near-flat coverage against 0% for both. Together these show large smooth dome panels with little grain, so some flat fills remain. Overall it is clean and readable but visibly flatter and thinner than the Beodeul references, so it falls short of the bar.
